item.title: Pastor Adam Hamilton could be Kansas's 1st Democratic senator since the Depression
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
When it comes to picking senators, no state is nearly as consistent as Kansas. The last Democrat to win there, a former county attorney named George McGill, was elected in 1932. Kansas's other senator, a Republican incumbent, won reelection in 1936. McGill lost to a Republican in 1938. And Kansas has been sending Republicans to the U.S. Senate ever since. That's a 90-year winning streak. But the composition of Kansas's Senate delegation could change on Nov. 3 — and with it, Republican control of the chamber as a whole. To the surprise of pretty much the entire political world, first-term GOP incumbent Roger Marshall is currently locked in a too-close-to-call contest with megachurch-pastor-turned-rookie-candidate Adam Hamilton — a former Republican who considered running as an independent before deciding to seek the Sunflower State's Democratic nomination. Hamilton, 61, is one of several heartland Democrats or Democratic-leaning independents who are giving Senate Republicans a run for their money in ruby-red states that President Trump won by double-digit margins in 2024 (including Texas, Iowa, Nebraska and even South Carolina ). He describes himself as " a liberal conservative and a conservative liberal ." "I'm not somebody who favors the Socialist Party," Hamilton said Wednesday night during a debate against Marshall. "I'm somebody who stands in the middle. I'm going to try to work for all Kansans, Republicans, independents and Democrats." Here's everything you need to know about one of the key figures of the 2026 midterms. Yahoo Who is Adam Hamilton? In some ways, Hamilton is similar to James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee in Texas , who is equally unapologetic about his Christian faith. But where Talarico has studied at seminary on the side — his main gig has been serving in the Texas House of Representatives — Hamilton is a bona fide church leader. Born in 1964 and raised in the Kansas City suburb of Prairie Village, Hamilton didn't go to church regularly as a child. His parents were teenage high school dropouts when they had him; they divorced by the time he was a teenager. Hamilton started drinking and taking drugs in seventh grade; two years later he got clean and started attending Pentecostal services on the recommendation of a door-to-door evangelist. Before long, Hamilton was heading up the church's youth group; he married a fellow attendee a week after high school graduation. Eventually, he earned a bachelor's degree in pastoral ministry from Oral Roberts University in Tulsa and a Master of Divinity from Southern Methodist University in Dallas. In 1990 — when Hamilton was just 25 — his United Methodist denomination tapped him to start a church for nonchurchgoers in suburban Kansas City. Worshippers initially met in the small chapel of a local funeral home. Today, Hamilton's United Methodist Church of the Resurrection is the largest United Methodist congregation in the U.S., with an average weekly attendance of about 25,000 people online, on television and across its nine area campuses. Its Christmas Eve offering, which is devoted to mission work, has topped $2 million . Hamilton has also written more than 30 books that have together sold millions of copies; his video-based lessons are used in Sunday school classes nationwide. In 2013, he preached at the National Prayer Service after President Barack Obama's second inauguration. Three years later, Obama appointed Hamilton to his Advisory Council on Faith-Based and Neighborhood Partnerships. Hamilton was registered as a Republican as recently as 2020; when he was first considering a 2026 Senate bid, he formed an exploratory committee as an independent. At the time he told his congregation — "a nearly equal mix of Republicans, Democrats and Independents," according to the Associated Press — that he could "bridge partisan divides in a highly polarized political climate" (as the AP put it). "Every week, it seemed there was another news story in the last year where I would find myself shaking my head and thinking, we have to do better," the self-described fifth-generation Kansan told the AP. But Hamilton was persuaded to run as a Democrat so as not to split the anti-Marshall vote in the general election. He wound up massively outraising his Democratic primary opponents and winning the party's Aug. 4 primary by more than 20 percentage points . What does Hamilton stand for? In college, Hamilton chose not to become a Pentecostal preacher because the denomination felt too black and white. In contrast, Methodism struck him as a thinking person's church, he told a local Kansas City paper in 2002 . "It seemed to me there was some gray in the world," Hamilton explained. "It is OK if you have doubts. It's OK if you have questions. We don't have to check our brains at the door." He now says he is an "independent-minded Democrat" who is "going to work across the aisle." At the Wednesday debate, Hamilton criticized Marshall for supporting the Trump administration's least-popular policies — tariffs, the war in Iran, immigration raids in farm country — while trying to distance himself from national Democrats. He called former President Joe Biden's immigration policy a "disaster," for instance, and promised not to "support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader if the Democrats [were] to control the Senate." When asked about transgender girls playing women's sports, Hamilton said he would not want his 12-year-old granddaughter competing against people assigned male at birth. "It's not a fair fight," he argued. Hamilton, left, and Republican Sen. Roger Marshall participate in a debate at WDAF TV in Kansas City, Mo. on Oct. 21, 2026. Charlie Riedel/AP via AP At times, Hamilton — who reminded the audience that he has "been a pastor for the last 38 years" and has "not been a senator" — struggled to provide specifics on issues such as farm subsidies, the Social Security wage cap and AI regulation, according to the New York Times . But Hamilton's general approach — his focus on "decency," affordability and "bringing people together" — has its roots in his ministry. Following the recent surge of federal immigration agents to Minneapolis, he cited on his podcast an Old Testament verse that commands Israelites to treat foreigners with love and fairness. In April, he said that he had voted against a state constitutional amendment that would have cleared the way for tougher abortion restrictions, arguing lawmakers should not be "the ethicists and the spiritual guides" for women (even as he lamented that his mother considered having an abortion when she was pregnant with him). And he has criticized Republican cuts to federal safety-net programs such as food stamps and Medicaid. "I just want to know, when did it become 'woke' to care for your neighbor?" Hamilton asked the AP , claiming that "Marshall would call [Jesus] 'woke'" if he were alive today. How could Hamilton perform in the midterms? Hamilton's local prominence, fundraising prowess, "centrist" message and skill on the stump have made this year's Kansas Senate contest very competitive. ("No one has more practice at extemporaneous talking than a megachurch pastor," the Times noted.) Marshall leads by 1 percentage point in the most recent poll to be released — but it's the only survey conducted over the last month that shows the Republican candidate ahead. The rest (save one tie) give Hamilton a slight edge (between 1 and 5 percentage points). Both candidates have faced controversy. Marshall has pushed back on reports that he sued hundreds of patients over unpaid medical bills during his decades-long career as an obstetrician-gynecologist, calling the allegations "blatant lies." And Hamilton has admitted he made a "mistake" by failing to bar a volunteer who had previously been accused of sexual abuse in 2005 from going on a retreat where he allegedly abused another boy. "I was actually preaching that weekend at Church of the Resurrection, and I did not sign off on him going back. I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back," Hamilton said during Wednesday's debate. "That was a mistake on my part. But I will tell you, when he was investigated the next year, we forbade him from working with youth or children anymore. He left our church angry and upset. And again, we played a critical role several years later in getting him arrested and convicted." Kansas hasn't sent a Democratic senator to Washington, D.C., since the Dust Bowl days — a conservative bent that's also reflected in its heavily Republican state legislature and the fact that it has voted Republican in every presidential election since 1940 except for Lyndon B. Johnson's 1964 landslide. But the state has elected two Democratic governors in recent years — Kathleen Sebelius (2003-2009) and term-limited incumbent Laura Kelly (2019-2027) — and there is a tradition of ticket-splitting that goes back even further. (Since 1957, neither major political party has held the Kansas governor's mansion for longer than eight consecutive years.) Could Hamilton benefit from that sort of checks-and-balances heterodoxy on Nov. 3? It's possible. In Wednesday's debate, Marshall embraced the Trump agenda and explicitly told viewers that "if you want [it] to continue, you need to come out, because we delivered on those things." But even in Kansas, 53% of likely voters currently disapprove of how the president is handling his job . The fate of Hamilton's campaign, and perhaps his party's hopes of winning the Senate, will turn on whether he can convince those voters to cast their ballots for him on Election Day — even if they haven't voted for a Democrat in a long, long time. item.title: Vivek Ramaswamy's $4 million attack ad against Amy Acton divides Ohio Republicans
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A new campaign ad in which the estranged mother of Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton argues that her daughter should not be elected as the Buckeye State's next governor has added a new level of controversy to what was already one of the most closely watched races of the midterms. Acton, a Democrat, is running to replace outgoing Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. She's facing Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a billionaire who ran an unsuccessful presidential campaign in 2024. In the ad, Acton's mother, Donna Arthur , calls her daughter a "liar" and urges Ohioans not to support her. "Don't let her become your governor," she says. "If you think she'll make your life better, you're fooling yourself. It will only get worse." As the ad began to spread across social media, Acton's brother released a statement in which he accused Arthur of siding with their stepfather after he was charged with sexually abusing Acton when she was a child, and criticized Ramaswamy for attempting to use the alleged abuse as a "political talking point." Ramaswamy defended the ad on Tuesday, telling reporters that Acton's account of her past "does deserve to be scrutinized." His campaign confirmed to the Enquirer that it will spend $4 million to air the ad across the state. The ongoing controversy over the ad, which has been widely condemned by Democrats and sparked pushback from some Republicans, has put a new spotlight on the race for Ohio's top elected office. Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, an incumbent Republican locked in a tight reelection race, released a statement saying he personally "would not have run" the ad. Meanwhile, Vice President JD Vance, himself a former senator from Ohio, said Republicans who disapprove of the ad should " stop whining " and remember that politics is a "tough business" during a campaign stop in Cincinnati on Wednesday. DeWine, who has endorsed Ramaswamy in the race, made his first public comments on the ad on Thursday, telling reporters that it was "wrong." "The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling, but when you know the rest of the story … it just makes it more wrong," he said. "It's wrong to run this ad." Trump weighed in on the controversy on Thursday, praising Arthur for her “courage.” “What she was really doing was saving Ohio from making a truly horrible choice!” He wrote on Truth Social. “The Press is trying to convince everyone that this Ad is bad, because it’s so good! Who wouldn’t use such an Ad? I would, it’s called, ‘hitting pay dirt.’” Yahoo Once a key swing state, Ohio has steadily become redder in recent decades. Four years ago, DeWine won reelection by more than 25 percentage points . But polls suggest that Acton has a chance to break the GOP's long run of control over the Ohio Statehouse. Here's what you need to know about who she is, how her past informs what she stands for today and what the polls say about her chances of winning. Who is Amy Acton? Acton has been open about the "difficult" childhood she endured growing up in Youngstown, Ohio, in the 1970s. On her campaign website, she says she overcame "periods of abuse, hunger, and neglect, and even wound up living in a tent in the middle of winter." In 2019, she publicly alleged for the first time that she had been sexually assaulted by her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, between the ages of 9 and 12. After Acton's biological father reported the alleged abuse in 1978, Arthur was arrested and charged with rape, according to contemporary news reports and court documents obtained by the Associated Press . Acton's mother sided with her stepfather, disputing the allegations. The couple left the state before Arthur could face trial and reportedly remained together until his death in 2004 . Both Acton and her mother say they have not seen or spoken to each other since a court hearing in which Acton testified against her stepfather nearly 50 years ago. "In the courthouse after they were charged, I went to give her a kiss, and she just turned her cheek away. That was the last time I ever saw her," Acton told the now-shuttered newspaper the Vindicator in 2019. Acton found more stability after moving in with her father and became a standout student in high school. She earned a bachelor's degree from Youngstown State University and a medical degree from the Northeast Ohio School of Medicine, working various jobs to pay her way through college. She completed residencies in pediatrics and preventive medicine before becoming a professor at Ohio State University , where she taught classes on maternal and child health. She also directed a community organization called Project L.O.V.E. to promote preventive health care among Columbus-area children. In 2019, DeWine tapped her to become director of the Ohio Department of Health. When the COVID-19 pandemic hit a year later, she advised DeWine to take swift action to control the spread of the virus. Under her guidance, Ohio became the first state in the nation to shut down all public schools. Acton also gained national attention thanks to the daily public briefings she gave throughout the early stages of the pandemic. In May 2020, an opinion piece in the New York Times called her "The Leader We Wish We All Had." Acton resigned a month later amid pressure from the Republican-led state legislature to sign orders rolling back COVID restrictions, moves she would later say "there was no science for." She briefly remained part of DeWine's administration as a public health adviser before leaving to resume working in the nonprofit sector. She announced her plans to run for governor in early 2025 and cruised through the Democratic primary in May. Acton was married to her first husband, with whom she had three children, for nearly 20 years before they divorced in 2008. She married her current husband in 2010 and became stepmother to his three children. What does Acton stand for? As a Democrat running in a conservative-leaning state, Acton fits firmly into the moderate wing of her party. Her policy platform focuses heavily on affordability, including proposals to lower the cost of health care, combat fraud, cut high energy bills and crack down on corporations that take advantage of workers and consumers. In July, she drew criticism from some progressive Democrats for saying that she supported barring transgender children from participating in girls' and women's sports. Soon afterward, she added language to her website pledging to protect Ohio's LGBTQ community, without directly contradicting her previously stated stance on transgender athletes' participation in sports. Acton has also spoken in favor of Ohio's voter ID requirements, a position that puts her at odds with many Democrats who view such laws as a voter suppression tactic by Republicans. Acton has also called for an increase in funding for police departments, more money for public schools and heavy investment in Ohio's rural and farming communities. What are her chances? Polling in the Ohio governor's race has fluctuated significantly as Election Day has grown closer. In the aggregate, the polls suggest that Acton has steadily widened her lead over Ramaswamy over the past several weeks. At the same time, two polls released in October show Ramaswamy ahead. The Cook Political Report and the Center for Politics , two of the country's top nonpartisan forecasters, list the race as a toss-up. No polls of the race have been conducted since the ad featuring Acton's mother became public, so it's too early to gauge what impact — if any — the controversy might have on voters' views of the two candidates. item.title: First-of-its-kind cancer vaccine cuts risk of melanoma returning by 42% in major trial
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — A first-of-its-kind cancer vaccine is significantly reducing the chances that melanoma patients’ tumors come back, according to results of a major study released Thursday by drugmakers Moderna and Merck. The vaccine was custom-brewed for each patient to match their tumor. Adding it to a standard post-surgery treatment reduced by 42% the risk of melanoma returning two years after surgery, according to the most advanced study to date of this new strategy for fighting cancer. “The field has been looking for a win and I think this one is a big one,” said Dr. Hussein Tawbi of MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, one of the researchers in the international study. The vaccine, called intismeran, is made with the same Nobel Prize-winning mRNA technology that was behind COVID-19 vaccines. Experimental personalized cancer vaccines made with mRNA and some other approaches also are being tested against other types of cancer including lung, kidney and pancreatic. Experts not involved with the new study say its success bolsters the field. “This is a new frontier,” said Karen Knudsen, CEO of the Parker Institute, which helps fund cancer immunotherapy research. “It’s a big step forward for science, for oncology, because this vaccine will apply to many different cancers,” said Dr. Michael Atkins, deputy director of Georgetown University’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. Moderna and Merck had announced in August that the late-stage trial of intismeran was successful but the detailed results were set to be released Saturday at a meeting of the European Society of Medical Oncology in Madrid. Some of the data was leaked publicly late Thursday, prompting a full release ahead of the weekend's scientific presentation. Most people think of vaccines as preventing an infection, like measles or whooping cough. There are already two cancer-preventing vaccines, the HPV and hepatitis B shots that block infection from those tumor-causing viruses. And research is underway to prevent some types of inherited cancer such as Lynch syndrome-caused colorectal cancer. But a personalized vaccine designed to block surgically-removed cancer from returning is very different. For the intismeran study, scientists hunted gene mutations unique to each patient’s tumor, mutations that create proteins which shouldn’t be in the body unless those cancer cells start to grow again. The custom vaccine — nine doses given three weeks apart — teaches the patient’s immune system to watch out for and attack those so-called neoantigens. How did it work? The study included more than 1,100 people with high-risk melanoma that was surgically removed. Everyone was given the standard follow-up therapy: Merck’s immunotherapy named Keytruda. The participants were randomly assigned to also receive custom-brewed vaccine doses or a placebo. Two years later, 82% of the people in the vaccine group were still living without a recurrence of their cancer compared to 70% who had gotten standard Keytruda alone. The trial is continuing to track participants’ longer-term outcomes. In 2024, Tony Hout joined the vaccine trial at MD Anderson after seeking care for a spot on his ear that had been bleeding intermittently and wouldn’t fully heal. Doctors recognized melanoma and during surgery discovered it had started to spread. “I want to make sure I’m doing everything I can to be here for my family,” said Hout, 62, who has since moved to Cayuga, Indiana, and travels back to Houston every few months for a study check-up. Scans this week showed he’s still cancer-free. The vaccine’s side effects were mainly the sore arm, fatigue and other reactions typical of mRNA coronavirus vaccination, MD Anderson's Tawbi said. Moderna and Merck are talking with regulatory authorities about next steps for seeking approval of the vaccine. Customized medicines generally are very expensive. The drugmakers aren’t discussing what such a cancer vaccine might cost. But Moderna President Stephen Hoge said the company’s special cancer vaccine manufacturing facility in Massachusetts is providing doses for thousands of people enrolled in multiple studies underway internationally. item.title: Supreme Court sides with Republicans in New Hampshire student ID voting fight
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON – The Supreme Court said New Hampshire can fully enforce a ban on voters using student IDs as a form of identification at the polls next month, a win for the Republican Party's effort to tighten voting procedures. The court on Oct. 22 agreed to pause a lower court’s ruling that a student ID is among the forms of identification that may be considered by poll workers if the voter lacks an approved government-issued ID. The state's U.S. Senate race is among the contests that will decide whether Republicans keep control of that chamber after the midterm elections. The Republican National Committee had backed the state's unsuccessful emergency appeal to the Supreme Court . New Hampshire, controlled by Republicans, is among several states that have banned registered voters from using a student ID to verify their identity at the polls. A voting-rights group challenged the change as discrimination against younger voters and as an unconstitutional burden on their right to vote. A federal judge in New Hampshire declined to block enforcement of the law as the case is litigated. But the judge also said the new law had not changed the fact that a poll worker may accept or reject a student ID as a valid form of identification on a case-by-case basis through the state’s "safety-valve" provision. New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan asked the Supreme Court to intervene. Scanlan, a Republican, said the judge's Oct. 2 order injected uncertainty into the state’s voting procedures less than three weeks before the election. He also said the judge wrongly interpreted the state's law. Coalition for Open Democracy, the group challenging the law, said the judge correctly concluded that state officials failed to identify "any security or integrity concerns specific to student ID cards and why they are unique among other non-governmental forms of identification" that are allowed on a case-by-case basis. The judge also found that the change had already kept one student from voting and could affect more because young voters may not have the government-issued IDs that are automatically accepted. In the brief and unsigned opinion, the Supreme Court pointed to its previous rulings that federal courts should not alter rules on the eve of an election. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice to publicly disagree with that decision. She said the federal judge had not changed the rules but only corrected the secretary of state's misinterpretation of them. "I respectfully dissent because − even, and perhaps especially, when an election is looming − I would not disturb aclearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State'selectoral processes," she wrote. item.title: Meta struck an unusual deal to keep Mark Zuckerberg from leaving California
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Meta Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg has made a deal with the firm's board allowing him to sell or transfer up to 20% of the company's new Class C stock so that his voting majority doesn't decrease even if he has to pay the billionaire tax. (Nic Coury / Associated Press ) Meta’s Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg has wielded enormous power over the social media empire he built more than two decades ago, leading the California juggernaut through major scandals, scrutiny and technological shifts. But the 42-year-old tech mogul considered leaving the state because he feared that a ballot measure to impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of California billionaires could reduce the amount of control he has over Meta, a recent regulatory filing shows. Meta’s board struck a deal so he would stay in California. Meta is the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. The filing highlights how one of the world’s wealthiest people, whose net worth totals more than $200 billion, is bracing for the possibility that California voters pass Proposition 40, a wealth tax proposal that would primarily be used to fund healthcare. Although supporters say the fear that billionaires will flee the state are overblown, the ultrawealthy have made moves to potentially avoid paying the tax or are funding campaigns to defeat it. Read more: Your guide to Proposition 40: California's billionaire tax proposal Zuckerberg’s influence over Meta is partly tied to how the company structures its stock. Zuckerberg holds roughly 60% of voting power over Meta even though he only owns about 13% of the company’s total shares. Meta has a dual-class share structure, dividing the stock into Class A shares with one vote each and Class B shares with 10 votes each. Zuckerberg holds a large amount of Class B stock, which gives him majority control over company decisions. If the wealth tax proposal passes, Zuckerberg is worried that it could reduce his voting power, according to the filing. The tech executive makes an annual salary of $1, so most of his wealth is linked to his stake in Meta. If he had to sell his Class B shares to pay the tax, that would reduce his voting majority in the company, according to the filing. In September, he told Meta’s board that he planned to list his Palo Alto home for sale, pressuring board members to find a solution. On Wednesday, Meta announced a new class of stock with no voting rights called Class C that would take effect in January. As part of the deal, Zuckerberg could sell or transfer up to 20% of Class C stock so his voting majority doesn’t decrease even if he has to pay the tax. “Mr. Zuckerberg’s continued leadership role in our Company, and his continuing presence at the Company’s headquarters in California, is critical at this current inflection point for the Company and the tech industry in order to continue to provide value-maximization for all shareholders,” the filing said. Since the company’s public debut, its share price has risen more than 1,700%, outperforming the S&P 500. In Meta’s third-quarter earnings call Wednesday, Chief Financial Officer Susan Li said creating a new class of nonvoting stock benefits the company in various ways, including “capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, other general corporate purposes.” “We believe this share class will maintain our founder-led structure. It will expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business driven by AI,” she said. Meta has roughly 66,700 workers globally. Its sprawling headquarters is in Menlo Park. Some billionaires such as Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey, Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen and Google co-founder Sergey Brin have opposed the wealth tax proposal. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, on the other hand, has said he doesn’t mind paying more taxes. The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West is backing the wealth tax proposal and says it applies to roughly 200 billionaires who have resided in California as of January 1, 2026, and could raise $100 billion. More than $300 million has been contributed to fight the billionaire tax, including two propositions that could block it if they gather more votes. Although stock prices fluctuate, Zuckerberg could face a tax liability of roughly $12 billion based on his net worth. In 2015, Zuckerberg and his wife, Dr. Priscilla Chan, pledged to give away 99% of his Facebook shares over their lifetimes when they celebrated the birth of their first daughter. The couple created the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, a philanthropic organization whose efforts include curing, managing and preventing all diseases. Although Zuckerberg lives in Palo Alto, he also owns real estate elsewhere, including in Hawaii, Washington, D.C. and Ireland. Times data journalist Gabrielle LaMarr LeMee contributed to this report. item.title: DOJ investigating Corey Lewandowski's role in DHS contracting under Kristi Noem
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Corey Lewandowski speaks to the press in July 2024..(Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images) - Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Justice Department prosecutors are investigating allegations of contract misconduct at the Department of Homeland Security, including the role of Corey Lewandowski who worked as de facto chief of staff to former Secretary Kristi Noem, according to multiple people familiar with the investigation. The probe follows a criminal referral for Lewandowski from the DHS Inspector General’s office, which has been examining contracting practices at the agency during Noem’s and Lewandowski’s tenure, according to one of the people familiar. The Justice Department declined to comment on the matter. “Mr. Lewandowski has not been contacted by the Justice Department regarding any investigation, and he denies any wrongdoing when he was proudly serving his country in a voluntary capacity,” Lewandowski’s attorney Adam Trigg told CNN. The Department of Homeland Security didn’t immediately return a request for comment on the matter. The referral is an unusual move for the Trump administration, which has been hesitant to criminally investigate its own members. Critics have instead largely accused the Justice Department of improperly targeting the president’s political enemies and accused DHS of protecting their own employees from scrutiny. In recent months, as the allegations of possible corruption emerged, Washington, DC, US Attorney Jeanine Pirro told officials in her office that she wanted investigators to look into claims of kickbacks connected to contracting at DHS, according to a second source familiar with the investigation. It’s still not clear which US Attorney’s office is leading the investigation. Prosecutors have been awaiting results from the DHS inspector general probe, the person familiar with the probe said. Lewandowski, a Republican operative, became a fixture at DHS early in President Donald Trump’s second term, serving as Noem’s chief adviser. But on paper, he was originally tapped to serve as a special government employee — a unique role meant to span a limited number of days. Lewandowksi’s straddling of senior government functions at DHS and service as a special government employee was uncharted territory, according to multiple people who spoke with CNN. Homeland Security officials ultimately viewed Lewandowski, a Trump ally, as Noem’s gatekeeper. He left the department when Trump fired Noem. Noem’s handling of contracts within DHS was one of the main catalysts for her ouster by Trump earlier this year, notably when she claimed that Trump knew of a $220 million ad campaign prominently featuring the secretary. During her tenure, Noem also tightened her grip on her department’s purse strings, ordering that every contract and grant over $100,000 had to cross her desk for approval — a move that Noem frequently defended as intended to cut down on waste but that multiple Homeland Security officials found unusual and unnecessary. The inspector general, Joseph Cuffari, complained to Congress in early March that Homeland Security leadership had been obstructing some of his work. Trump, when asked by a reporter on Thursday about the Lewandowski investigation, said he didn’t know much about it as he only just learned of it. He repeatedly said, however, that if people working for him are dishonest, he wants them prosecuted. “They’re stealing from me, so I want my people to be honest,” Trump said. “And if they’re not honest, I’ll have my DOJ go and do whatever they have to do.” This story has been updated with additional details.
